isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.response: Rabbi Tovia Singer and Jews for Judaism answer that Christians quote these sources selectively. The Targum does apply the servant's exaltation to the Messiah. But it moves all the suffering onto Israel and the nations. Read whole, they say, it argues against a suffering Messiah rather than for one. Passages like Sanhedrin 98b are aggadah — homily and wordplay, not careful interpretation. Midrash regularly applies a verse to several different figures without settling its plain meaning. And the main medieval commentators — Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak — all read the servant as Israel. That fits Isaiah's own habit of calling Israel 'my servant' in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. A tradition's sermons, they conclude, do not overturn its scholarship.
isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.rationale: One narrow fact is agreed on all sides. Messianic readings of Isaiah 53 — including readings where the Messiah suffers — do exist in older Jewish literature. What is argued about is how much weight they carry, not whether they are there. So use the claim in exactly that form. Not 'the rabbis agree with us.' Instead: 'reading this chapter as one individual Messiah is a Jewish option, and it is an old one.' That is enough to move the conversation, and it is all the evidence supports. Overstating it hands Singer an easy correction, and he has a prepared one.
isaiah-53-rabbinic-messianic-reading.claim: People often say that only Christians read Isaiah 53 as being about one individual Messiah. Classical Jewish sources say otherwise. Targum Jonathan, the official Aramaic paraphrase, opens the passage: 'Behold, my servant the Messiah shall prosper.' The Talmud asks what the Messiah's name is, and one answer cites Isaiah 53:4 — 'surely he has borne our griefs' (Sanhedrin 98b). Ruth Rabbah 5:6 applies Isaiah 53:5 to the Messiah's sufferings. An old Yom Kippur poem, preserved in Ashkenazi prayer books, speaks of 'our righteous anointed' who 'carries our sins.' The sixteenth-century commentator Moshe Alshich wrote that 'our rabbis with one voice' applied the passage to King Messiah. None of that proves Jesus is the Messiah. It does show that reading Isaiah 53 as one suffering individual is native to Jewish tradition, not a Christian import.

isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.response: The strongest reply comes from Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Tovia Singer. Isaiah has already named the servant — 'Israel, my servant' — in Isaiah 41:8, Isaiah 44:1 and Isaiah 49:3. So the burden falls on anyone claiming an individual. Who is speaking in chapter 53? On this reading, the gentile kings of Isaiah 52:15, stunned at Israel's vindication. Each king says 'my people' about his own nation. That dissolves the servant-versus-people problem at 53:8. They also argue that the Hebrew preposition in 53:5 means Israel suffered from the sins of the nations, not for them. National Israel dying and reviving is standard prophetic imagery — Ezekiel 37's dry bones do the same thing. And this is not a medieval invention: Origen records Jewish opponents arguing it around 248 AD.
isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.rationale: Graded strong for the Christian side on the narrow textual point. To make the collective reading work, you have to turn the gentile kings into the penitent confessors, and read 'my people' as meaning a different people in each king's mouth. Both readings strain the text. Isaiah 53:9 describes an individual grave, with 'a rich man in his death.' And the grammar of 53:5 runs the other way from the proposed reading: he was wounded for our transgressions, and the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all. That is the language of one bearing what belongs to others. Still, say plainly that Isaiah does call Israel his servant elsewhere. If you skip that, you look like you are hiding it.
isaiah-53-servant-distinct-from-israel.claim: Inside the passage itself, the servant cannot simply be the nation. He suffers 'for the transgression of my people' (Isaiah 53:8). That makes the servant and the people two parties, not one. He is innocent — 'he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth' (Isaiah 53:9). Isaiah's Israel is not innocent, and Isaiah says so repeatedly, including in the same chapter: 'all we like sheep have gone astray.' The servant is silent under suffering (Isaiah 53:7), while Israel's laments fill whole books. He dies — 'cut off out of the land of the living,' given a grave — and yet afterwards 'prolongs his days.' The Hebrew Bible promises that Israel as a nation never dies (Jeremiah 31:35-37). And his suffering achieves something for others: 'he shall bear their iniquities' (Isaiah 53:11). Earlier songs already describe a servant with a mission to Israel (Isaiah 49:5-6).

sukkah-52a-two-messiahs.response: The rabbinic answer is that Messiah son of Joseph is a warrior. He dies in the final battle against Gog. His death is not a sacrifice and accomplishes nothing redemptive. He also dies at the end of history, not centuries before the redemption. They add that the idea is post-biblical, marginal, and possibly a response to Bar Kokhba's death in 135 AD rather than ancient teaching. Above all, Maimonides' test stands. In the Mishneh Torah he says the Messiah is identified by what he achieves: a rebuilt Temple, the exiles gathered home, world peace, and everyone knowing God. Anyone who dies without doing those things is disqualified. Adding a second coming, they argue, is an unfalsifiable patch — and at least the rabbis' two Messiahs both act inside one redemption.
sukkah-52a-two-messiahs.rationale: Here is what is conceded. The tradition itself found a Messiah who is killed, in these texts. Sukkah 52a hangs his death on Zechariah 12:10 — the same verse John 19:37 quotes. Daniel Boyarin, a professor of Talmud and not a Christian, argues that suffering-Messiah ideas are thoroughly Jewish. Use this to change what the conversation is about. The question was never whether Judaism could imagine a Messiah who dies. It plainly could, and did. The question is whether the one who died is the one who returns. That is a much smaller disagreement than most Christians and most Jews assume they are having.
sukkah-52a-two-messiahs.claim: The Hebrew Bible gives two pictures of the coming one, and they resist being merged. One is a reigning king from David's line (Isaiah 9:6-7, Jeremiah 23:5-6, Zechariah 9:9-10). The other is a figure who suffers, is pierced, and dies (Isaiah 53, Zechariah 12:10, Psalm 22, Daniel 9:26). Rabbinic Judaism saw both and answered with two Messiahs. Messiah son of Joseph fights and is killed — the Talmud applies the mourning of Zechariah 12 to his death (Sukkah 52a). Messiah son of David then reigns. Later midrash goes further: Pesikta Rabbati 36-37 describes a Messiah who accepts crushing suffering for Israel's sins. So the two-Messiah scheme is the tradition's own admission that both pictures are in the text. The Christian claim has the same shape and needs one figure instead of two: suffering servant first, returning king second (Luke 24:26).

daniel-9-cut-off-before-destruction.response: There are two replies, and the second is much stronger. The traditional one: mashiach simply means an anointed person. Rashi reads the anointed one of verse 25 as Cyrus and the one in verse 26 as King Agrippa. The passage is about the Temple era, not a dying redeemer. The Talmud also curses those who calculate the end (Sanhedrin 97b), precisely because such maths produces false messiahs. The critical-scholarly reply is harder to answer. On that view Daniel 9 was written in the 160s BC. The anointed one 'cut off' is the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC, and the destroyer is Antiochus IV. The seventy weeks then end in the Maccabean crisis. On this reading the Christian count depends on picking a convenient starting decree and treating symbolic sabbatical numbers as exact solar years.
daniel-9-cut-off-before-destruction.rationale: Graded contested, because the Maccabean dating is the mainstream critical view and deserves to be named rather than ignored. But something usable survives every reading a Jewish friend is likely to hold. On the traditional Jewish chronology — Seder Olam and Rashi — the seventy weeks run out at 70 AD. So by the tradition's own arithmetic, whatever the passage is about, its clock stops at the destruction of the Temple. That is the version to use. Do not build an argument on a precise start date; you cannot defend it, and a prepared friend will know that.
daniel-9-cut-off-before-destruction.claim: Daniel 9:24-27 sets out seventy 'weeks' for Israel and Jerusalem — a period to 'finish transgression' and 'bring in everlasting righteousness.' The part that carries the argument needs no precise arithmetic. Daniel 9:26 says an anointed one shall be 'cut off and have nothing,' and that afterwards the people of a coming ruler 'shall destroy the city and the sanctuary.' Whatever counting scheme you use, the anointed one is cut off before the destruction. That destruction happened in AD 70. So the window closed then. Strikingly, traditional Jewish chronology agrees about the end point: Seder Olam Rabbah runs the 490 years to the Second Temple's destruction, and Rashi identifies the cut-off anointed one with Agrippa at that same moment. Jesus was executed around AD 30, inside the last generation of the standing Temple. Josephus records that an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures fed expectation that the time had come.

micah-5-2-bethlehem.response: The counter-missionary reading is that Micah names Bethlehem as the clan seat of David's family. 'From you' addresses the family stock — Ephrathah is David's clan, as in Ruth 4:11 and 1 Samuel 17:12. So the verse predicts a ruler descended from David, not a birthplace requirement. On that reading, 'origins from of old' means his family line reaches far back, not that he existed before he was born. They add that applying it to Jesus cannot be checked. The two birth accounts differ — Matthew has a flight to Egypt under Herod, Luke a census under Quirinius a decade later. The census mechanism itself is historically doubtful. And skeptics argue Bethlehem was written into the story because the prophecy was known.
micah-5-2-bethlehem.rationale: The identification itself — that this verse is about the Messiah — is granted by the classical Jewish sources. That part is solid and worth establishing early, because it means both traditions agree that messianic prophecy with checkable content exists. What is genuinely contested is applying it to Jesus, which depends on the birth narratives, and on a reading of 'from everlasting' that the Hebrew does not force. Use the verse to establish the category. Do not use it as proof on its own.
micah-5-2-bethlehem.claim: Micah 5:2 reads: 'You, Bethlehem Ephrathah, little among the clans of Judah — from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.' That this verse is about the Messiah is not disputed between the two traditions. Targum Jonathan renders it 'from you shall come forth before Me the Messiah.' Rashi writes 'from you shall emerge for Me Messiah son of David.' The Gospels record the same thing as the standard Jewish answer to where the Messiah would be born (Matthew 2:4-6, John 7:42). Jesus's birth in Bethlehem is reported in both birth narratives, which are otherwise independent of each other. For Christian readers the phrase 'origins from of old' points past ancestry, and fits the child called 'mighty God' in Isaiah 9:6.

zechariah-12-10-pierced.response: The strongest reply comes from Tovia Singer, Rashi and the NJPS translation. The speaker is God — 'they shall look to Me' — and God cannot be pierced. The Hebrew daqar here means slain in battle. So the verse describes national mourning at the end of history, over those who fell in the war of Gog and Magog. NJPS renders it 'they shall lament to Me about those who are slain.' The phrase 'et asher' can mean 'concerning him whom,' which removes the paradox of a pierced God entirely. Rashi does cite the Messiah son of Joseph tradition, but as aggadah about a warrior killed at history's end — not an atoning death under Rome. And some Hebrew manuscripts read 'look to him' rather than 'to me,' which takes away the Christian pivot altogether.
zechariah-12-10-pierced.rationale: Graded conceded on the key point. The Talmud itself connects this verse's mourning to a Messiah who is killed, at Sukkah 52a — the same connection John 19:37 makes. That agreement, coming from sources with no reason to help Christians, is what gives this entry its force. Handle the 'me' versus 'him' question with complete honesty. The standard Hebrew text reads 'to me,' which is the harder and better-attested reading, and Christians should say so rather than reaching for the manuscripts that make life easier.
zechariah-12-10-pierced.claim: Zechariah 12:10 says: 'They shall look to me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him as one mourns for an only son.' That switch — look to me, mourn for him — is in the Hebrew itself, not in the translation. The decisive piece comes from the Talmud. Sukkah 52a asks what the great mourning of Zechariah 12 is for. The accepted answer applies it to Messiah son of Joseph, who is slain, and quotes this very verse. So the classical Jewish reading closest to the plain sense already found a pierced, slain, mourned Messiah here. John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion. The setting fits with unusual precision: the house of David and the people of Jerusalem looking in grief at one they pierced, with a fountain 'opened for sin' in the next verse.

psalm-22-pierced-hands-feet.response: The reply is that ka'aru is not a known Hebrew verb for piercing. The root means 'dig,' and 'they dug my hands and my feet' is strained. The standard Hebrew — 'like a lion at my hands and feet' — fits the psalm's animal imagery, which already has bulls, dogs and lions. The psalm is David's own lament, written in the past tense, with no messianic label attached. Midrash Tehillim applies it to Esther. They also argue the Gospel writers shaped the passion account on the psalm, which would explain the fit. And one detail lands hard: the New Testament never quotes verse 16. If 'they pierced my hands and my feet' were decisive, the evangelists somehow missed it. Nothing in the psalm teaches atonement for others.
psalm-22-pierced-hands-feet.rationale: Graded contested, with full honesty. The textual evidence — the Septuagint and the Nahal Hever fragment — genuinely supports an ancient verb here, and it refutes the charge that Christians invented the reading. But whether that verb means 'pierced' is uncertain, and the New Testament's silence about verse 16 is a real fact that an informed friend will raise. Concede it before they do. Then read the rest of the psalm, which needs no argument at all: the mocking in verses 7 and 8, and the clothing divided by lot in verse 18.
psalm-22-pierced-hands-feet.claim: Psalm 22 reads like an eyewitness account of a crucifixion. It opens 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — the words Jesus quoted (Matthew 27:46). Mockers shake their heads and say 'he trusted in the LORD, let him deliver him' (verses 7-8). 'They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots' (verse 18). And it ends not in death but in worldwide praise: 'all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD.' Verse 16 is the famous problem. The standard Hebrew text reads ka'ari — 'like a lion my hands and my feet,' with no verb at all. The pre-Christian Greek Septuagint reads 'they pierced my hands and feet.' And the Nahal Hever Psalms scroll, a Jewish manuscript from the first century AD, has the verb form. So the 'pierced' reading is ancient and Jewish. What it means is still debated.

genesis-49-10-shiloh.response: This reply has real teeth. If 'sceptre' means political sovereignty, it left Judah at the Babylonian exile in 586 BC, and stayed gone through Persian, Greek and Hasmonean rule — and the Hasmoneans were Levites, not Judahites. All of that is centuries before Jesus, so the popular 'it departed in AD 6' clock looks arbitrary. Rabbinic reading takes shevet as tribal identity and internal authority — the exilarchs, the patriarchs, the courts — which continued long after 70 AD. The phrase 'ad ki' can mean 'even when,' not 'until.' And 'Shiloh' itself is obscure: possibly the place name, possibly 'tribute to him.' Building a timetable on an uncertain word is unsound. The messianic reading in Targum Onkelos names the ultimate figure without conceding any first-century deadline.
genesis-49-10-shiloh.rationale: This one splits in practice, so treat the halves differently. The messianic identification of Shiloh is conceded — Onkelos, Sanhedrin 98b and Rashi all make it, and those are common ground worth citing. But the popular Christian timing argument is contested and half-broken. The claim that the sceptre departed when the Sanhedrin lost the power of capital punishment ignores the Babylonian exile, which removed Judah's sovereignty far earlier. Use the identification. Drop the clock.
genesis-49-10-shiloh.claim: Jacob's blessing over Judah says: 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples' (Genesis 49:10). Once again the messianic reading is native to Jewish tradition. Targum Onkelos renders it 'until the Messiah comes, whose is the kingdom.' Sanhedrin 98b lists 'Shiloh' among the Messiah's names. Rashi glosses it 'the King Messiah, to whom the kingdom belongs.' So the Torah itself, read with rabbinic agreement, points to a specific individual at the end of Judah's line — one who commands the obedience not of Israel only but of 'the peoples,' plural. Christians add that Judah's remaining self-rule, the Sanhedrin's power over capital cases, lapsed under Rome in the generation before AD 70. Avodah Zarah 8b records capital cases ceasing 'forty years before the destruction.'

isaiah-7-14-almah.response: This reply is ancient and strong. Trypho was already making it to Justin Martyr around 160 AD. The Hebrew word is almah, a young woman. The sign is given to King Ahaz during a crisis in 734 BC, and it is useless to him if it happens seven centuries later. Verse 16 ties the child's early years to the fall of Rezin and Pekah. The child may well be Isaiah's own son — Isaiah 8:3-4 gives a boy with the identical timetable. They also note that parthenos in the Septuagint does not have to mean virgin technically: Dinah is called parthenos in Genesis 34:3 after she has been violated. So Matthew, reading Greek, built a doctrine on a translation choice. Later Jewish translators — Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion — rendered it 'young woman,' correcting rather than conspiring.
isaiah-7-14-almah.rationale: Graded weak for the Christian side, and saying so is this entry's main job. Isaiah 7:14 is not evidence for the virgin birth. It is Matthew thinking about a virgin birth he already believed for other reasons, using pattern-fulfilment — a normal Jewish reading technique of his day. Never open with this verse. Never present it as proof. Giving it away honestly is exactly what earns you a hearing on Isaiah 53 and Daniel 9, which do hold.
isaiah-7-14-almah.claim: Isaiah 7:14 says: 'The almah shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.' Matthew 1:23 quotes it for the virgin birth, using the Greek Septuagint's word parthenos. Here are the honest facts. Almah means a young woman of marrying age, as in Genesis 24:43 and Exodus 2:8. It is not the technical word for virgin, which is betulah. And the sign is given to King Ahaz with a short horizon — before the child knows good from evil, the two kings threatening him will be gone (Isaiah 7:15-16). Here is what Christians can still say. Jewish translators in Alexandria chose parthenos two centuries before Jesus, so that reading predates Christianity. The Immanuel child runs forward into Isaiah 8 and the divine child of Isaiah 9:6. And Matthew's word for 'fulfil' regularly means filling out a pattern, not bare prediction — he uses it the same way of Hosea 11:1 in Matthew 2:15.

second-temple-messianic-expectation.response: The reply concedes the expectation and then turns it around. Yes, first-century Judea was full of messianic hope. That is precisely why there were so many claimants — Theudas, the Egyptian, later Bar Kokhba — and all of them failed the same test. The dominant expectation was a royal, national deliverer: Psalms of Solomon 17 describes a conquering king who purges Jerusalem of gentiles. As for 4Q521, it is fragmentary, and its wonder-worker may be describing God's own acts rather than the Messiah's. On this reading Jesus matched the minor motifs and failed the central ones. No throne. No exiles gathered. No peace. No rebuilt Temple. And the era's fever, as Sanhedrin 97b warns, is exactly what produced the false-messiah problem.
second-temple-messianic-expectation.rationale: The conceded fact is powerful on its own. We have datable, pre-Christian, Jewish texts expecting an anointed one who heals, raises the dead and preaches good news to the poor. Luke 7:22 has Jesus answering John's question — 'are you the one?' — in exactly that vocabulary. Make 4Q521 the centrepiece. It cannot be a Christian forgery, because it was sealed in a cave before Jesus was born. That single fact removes the 'you invented it afterwards' objection permanently.
second-temple-messianic-expectation.claim: The charge that Christians read a Messiah back into neutral texts fails on pre-Christian evidence. The Dead Sea Scroll 4Q521, from the first century BC, says of the messianic age: 'the heavens and the earth will obey His Messiah… he will heal the badly wounded, he will revive the dead, he will proclaim good news to the poor.' That is strikingly close to how Jesus answers John the Baptist in Luke 7:22 — including raising the dead, which is not in the Isaiah passages underneath. Psalms of Solomon 17, from the mid first century BC, prays for the 'son of David' who will reign as 'Lord Messiah.' Qumran expected both priestly and royal anointed figures. Josephus records an 'ambiguous oracle' in the scriptures convincing many that a world ruler would arise from Judea in that era. The expectation was alive, textual, and clustered exactly in Jesus's generation.

jeremiah-31-new-covenant.response: The reply is: read the content. The new covenant is the same Torah — God says 'I will put my Torah within them' — written so deeply inside people that it can no longer be broken. Nothing here abolishes the commandments, replaces Israel, or mentions a mediator who dies. They also note that chadashah can mean renewed, the way the moon is renewed each month. And the timeframe is the messianic age, when 'they shall all know me' — which is plainly not the present world. Then comes their strongest move. The very next verses, Jeremiah 31:35-37, stake God's own reliability on Israel remaining a nation forever. That is the most powerful anti-replacement passage in the Bible, and it sits inside the passage Christians are quoting. If the church reads verses 31 to 34 literally, it must read 35 to 37 the same way.
jeremiah-31-new-covenant.rationale: Strong for the Christian side on the narrow claim. The Hebrew Bible itself expects a new covenant, grounded in final forgiveness, promised to Israel. Christians did not invent the category — they claim it. But notice what the reply actually defeats. It defeats the overreach: that the Torah was abolished, or that Israel was replaced. Anyone using this entry has to renounce that overreach too, because Jeremiah 31:35-37 is in the same passage and says the opposite. So use it in both directions. It answers the charge that Christians made up a second covenant, and it rebukes any Christian who thinks God is finished with Israel.
jeremiah-31-new-covenant.claim: The phrase 'new covenant' — in Hebrew brit chadashah — is not a Christian invention. It appears in the Hebrew Bible, at Jeremiah 31:31-34. "Behold, days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah — not like the covenant I made with their fathers, which they broke." Its content is spelled out: the Torah written on hearts, everyone knowing the LORD directly, and at the climax, 'I will forgive their iniquity, and remember their sin no more.' The promise assumes the covenant at Sinai could be broken, and was. It then announces a covenant built on final forgiveness. The New Testament stakes its whole self-understanding on this text: 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20), argued at length in Hebrews 8-10. Ezekiel 36:25-27 promises something parallel. Whatever you conclude about Jesus, the category belongs to Jeremiah, not to Paul.

yoma-39b-forty-years.response: The reply is that this is aggadah — remembered homily, written down centuries after the events. 'Forty years' is the stock biblical and rabbinic number for a generation: the wilderness, Eli, David. The same tractate says the crimson thread had already been failing intermittently generations earlier, after Shimon HaTzaddik. And the rabbis give their own reason for God's favour being withdrawn, plainly and internally: the sins of that era, especially baseless hatred (Yoma 9b) and the corruption of the later priesthood. The passage never mentions the rejection of a messianic claimant. Building date-dependent theology on a symbolic number, against the text's own stated explanation, is exactly the proof-texting Jewish readers recognise in missionary material.
yoma-39b-forty-years.rationale: Conceded, in the strict sense this section uses. The passage exists, it is Jewish, and it says what it says: the signs of divine acceptance failed for the Temple's last forty years, a span that lands around 30 AD. But carry the honesty with it. This is a suggestive convergence, not a proof. The number is schematic. And the passage supplies its own explanation, which is not the one Christians want. Present it as something striking worth explaining, and let your friend do the explaining.
yoma-39b-forty-years.claim: The Talmud records this: 'Forty years before the destruction of the Temple, the lot did not come up in the right hand; nor did the crimson-colored strap become white; nor did the westernmost lamp burn; and the doors of the Sanctuary opened by themselves' (Yoma 39b). The crimson thread turning white was the visible sign that the Day of Atonement had been accepted — the image comes from Isaiah 1:18, 'though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be white as snow.' The Temple fell in AD 70. Forty years earlier is about AD 30, the era of the crucifixion. On the Christian reading, the rabbis' own tradition remembers that from roughly the moment Jesus died, the signs of acceptance went dark, and stayed dark until the whole system ended. The same passage treats the failures as a mark of divine displeasure.

atonement-after-the-temple.response: This reply is substantial, and it is made from the Bible rather than around it. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly shows atonement without blood. A poor Israelite brings a flour sin-offering in Leviticus 5:11-13 — no blood at all — and 'the priest shall make atonement.' Hosea 14:2 prescribes the words of repentant lips instead of bulls. Solomon's dedication prayer in 1 Kings 8:46-50 anticipates forgiveness with no Temple, through repentant prayer. Daniel prayed without a Temple. Nineveh was forgiven for repentance alone in Jonah 3:10. Psalm 51:17 says the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. And Hosea 6:6 — 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' — was quoted by Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai after the Temple fell, and by Jesus in Matthew 9:13. Leviticus 17:11, they add, is about eating blood, not a monopoly on forgiveness.
atonement-after-the-temple.rationale: Graded contested, because this counter-case is real Bible rather than evasion. Flour offerings, Nineveh and Psalm 51 have to be conceded, and the claim that 'Judaism has no answer for sin' is simply false — this site should say so plainly. The genuinely open question is narrower, and worth asking carefully rather than triumphantly. The Torah's own centre of gravity for atonement is Yom Kippur, the altar and the blood. Judaism after 70 AD had to build a system without them. Asking where the Torah authorises that is a fair question. Claiming Judaism has nothing to say is not.
atonement-after-the-temple.claim: Leviticus grounds forgiveness in blood offered in place of the sinner: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls' (Leviticus 17:11). The Day of Atonement worked by blood carried into the holy place (Leviticus 16). In AD 70 the altar vanished, and with it the entire system the Torah lays out — for nineteen centuries and counting. Rabbinic Judaism answered with repentance, prayer and charity. The Christian claim is that the timing is not an accident. Within one generation of Jesus's death — which the New Testament presents as the sacrifice the whole system pointed to, and which Isaiah 53:10 calls a guilt offering — God let the shadow end because the substance had come. Hosea 3:4-5 describes the shape of the age: many days without king and without sacrifice, before Israel returns and seeks 'David their king.'

hosea-blindness-restoration-romans-11.response: The Jewish reply here is not about interpretation. It is historical, and it deserves full weight. Whatever Romans 11 says, nineteen centuries of Christendom said otherwise. Justin Martyr claimed Israel's inheritance for the church. Chrysostom preached against the synagogue. Crusaders massacred the Rhineland communities with Romans 11 sitting in their Bibles. Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies fed directly into the twentieth century. A charter that failed to restrain its own civilisation for most of its history can fairly be judged by its fruit — a test Jesus endorsed in Matthew 7:16. They add that even 'all Israel will be saved' has been read as meaning the church. A Jewish reader may reasonably conclude the text is ambiguous at best, and decoration at worst.
hosea-blindness-restoration-romans-11.rationale: Strong for the Christian side at the level of the text. The plain sense of Romans 11 condemns replacement theology and the contempt that grew from it. But the history of its violation is a history of Christians breaking their own scripture, and this entry has to say that in exactly those words. This is the entry that sets the posture for the whole section, and it goes first in any real conversation. In practice: open with confession, not with argument.
hosea-blindness-restoration-romans-11.claim: The Hebrew Bible itself describes a pattern for Israel. A long season without king or sacrifice, then a wholehearted return — 'afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God and David their king' (Hosea 3:4-5). A spirit of deep sleep and sealed vision that is later lifted (Isaiah 29:10-14). Scattering and regathering (Deuteronomy 30:1-6). The house of David looking on the pierced one and mourning, with a fountain opened for sin (Zechariah 12:10-13:1). Paul builds Romans 9-11 on exactly that pattern. Israel's present non-recognition of Jesus is 'partial and temporary' (Romans 11:25), and it ends with 'all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:26). The same chapter gives binding orders to gentile Christians: 'do not boast over the branches' (Romans 11:18). Israel remains 'beloved for the sake of the fathers,' and 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.' Christian contempt for Jews is not an excess of the system. It is disobedience to the system's own charter.

nt-jewish-library.response: The reply is that Jewish authorship does not make a book Jewish — Spinoza was a Jew too. The New Testament as it was finally canonised contains the seeds of the contempt. 'His blood be on us and on our children' in Matthew 27:25. 'You are of your father the devil' in John 8:44. 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16. A Jewish reader does not meet these as arguments inside a Jewish family. They meet them as the proof-texts of pogroms. The parting of the ways was real: whatever the first generation was, the church that carried these texts read them against Jews for eighteen centuries. And theologically, the New Testament's claims — incarnation, and a divine-human mediator who atones — cross lines drawn at Deuteronomy 6:4 and Numbers 23:19 that no amount of first-century context erases.
nt-jewish-library.rationale: Conceded. The Jewishness of Jesus and of the New Testament is now the mainstream view in critical scholarship, and Jewish scholars have led much of that work. Cite Geza Vermes, Amy-Jill Levine and Daniel Boyarin rather than Christian apologists — the point only works if the sources have no stake in it. Use this entry to change what the conversation is. You are not asking someone to convert to a gentile religion. You are asking them to consider a first-century Jewish claim about a Jewish figure, made by Jews.
nt-jewish-library.claim: Every New Testament author except probably Luke was a Jew. Its earliest community was a Torah-keeping Jerusalem congregation of 'many thousands of Jews… all zealous for the law' (Acts 21:20). Matthew builds his Gospel around five great discourses, echoing the five books of Moses, and presents Jesus as the greater Moses who came 'not to abolish the Torah or the Prophets… but to fulfil' (Matthew 5:17). Jesus's arguments — over divorce, Sabbath healing, hand-washing — run along recognised Pharisaic fault lines of his day. Paul calls himself a Pharisee in the present tense, decades after Damascus (Acts 23:6). This is now the mainstream of critical scholarship, and much of it is Jewish work: Geza Vermes's Jesus the Jew, E. P. Sanders, the Jewish Annotated New Testament edited by Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Brettler, and Daniel Boyarin, who argues that even the divine 'Son of Man' Messiah is a Jewish idea before it is a Christian one.

avoid-talmud-quote-mining.response: There is no steelman for fabrication. Here is the only honest residue. A few genuine Talmudic passages may argue against a figure some manuscripts call Yeshu. Scholars dispute whether that is Jesus of Nazareth at all — the chronological details are off by about a century. At most they show that Jews in late antiquity rejected Christian claims, which everybody already knew. And they were written under persecution by the church. Quoting them as ammunition means citing a wounded community's polemic while ignoring who wounded it.
avoid-talmud-quote-mining.rationale: Do not use this, and name the practice when you see it. The commandment against false witness applies to citations. A Christian who forwards a fabricated Talmud quote is bearing false witness against a neighbour, in Christ's name, in a genre with a body count — the Beilis trial, and Nazi reprints of Rohling. If a Talmud passage genuinely matters to your argument, the rule is simple: read it in context on Sefaria first, or do not use it.
avoid-talmud-quote-mining.claim: A body of fake and mangled 'Talmud quotes' has been circulating for three centuries. It runs from Eisenmenger in 1700, through August Rohling's Der Talmudjude in 1871 and Pranaitis's The Talmud Unmasked in 1892, to Elizabeth Dilling in 1964 — and now recycles endlessly online. Invented references. Mistranslations. Passages stripped of the context that reverses them, alleging the Talmud blesses deceiving gentiles or blasphemes Jesus and Mary. At the 1913 Beilis blood-libel trial, Pranaitis was destroyed under cross-examination, unable to answer basic questions about the Talmud. The genuine scholarly question about the few disputed 'Yeshu' passages is handled soberly in Peter Schäfer's Jesus in the Talmud: late texts, of contested reference, censored under Christian pressure, telling us about medieval conflict rather than first-century fact. Christians who pass on Talmud memes are laundering antisemitic forgeries into an evangelistic conversation.

avoid-jews-killed-jesus.response: There is no counter-argument to put at its strongest here. There is only an observation your Jewish friend will rightly press. The passion narratives themselves supplied the raw material — especially Matthew 27:25, and John's repeated use of 'the Jews.' Christian theology cannot fully hand the problem off to misreaders. A Christian who uses this framing has not merely made a tactical mistake. He has contradicted his own scriptures and stepped into the persecutors' line.
avoid-jews-killed-jesus.rationale: Do not use it, ever, in any form — including the softened versions, like 'your ancestors rejected him.' Theologically the Christian confession is that my sin required the cross. Every communion service says so. If the subject comes up, the Christian move is confession: the church's guilt for the deicide charge and everything it harvested. Then, only if invited, the history of who actually ordered the execution.
avoid-jews-killed-jesus.claim: The deicide charge is false by the New Testament's own account, and historically it is the deadliest sentence in Christian rhetoric. Start with the account. Crucifixion was a Roman penalty, carried out by Roman soldiers on a Roman prefect's verdict. The Jewish participants were a narrow Temple faction, not a people. Peter tells Jews in Jerusalem 'you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers' (Acts 3:17). Acts 4:27-28 names Herod, Pilate, the gentiles and Israel together. Isaiah 53:10 says 'it pleased the LORD to crush him.' And Jesus says 'no one takes my life from me — I lay it down of my own accord' (John 10:18). Now the history. Matthew 27:25, read as a blood-curse, underwrote Holy Week pogroms, expulsions and blood libels for centuries. The Catholic Church formally repudiated it in 1965: Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today.'

avoid-legalism-caricature.response: The only real pushback runs the other way. Some scholars in the 'new perspective' debate argue that E. P. Sanders overcorrected, and that Second Temple sources do contain strands where merit is weighed — 4 Ezra, for instance. That is true, and irrelevant to the practice this entry bans. Whatever the academic balance turns out to be, telling a Jewish friend her religion is loveless rule-keeping is false about the Judaism she actually lives — her Shabbat table, her liturgy of mercy, her grandmother's kindness. It also identifies the speaker instantly as someone who has never read a page of the prayer book.
avoid-legalism-caricature.rationale: Do not use it. It fails academically, after Sanders. It fails liturgically — read Avinu Malkeinu, which is a prayer for undeserved mercy. And it fails relationally, because it insults the hearer's own life. It also misreads Paul, whose argument in Romans 9-10 is about Israel and the Messiah, not about Jews lacking grace. Replace it with the honest dividing line this whole section is built on: both traditions believe in grace, and disagree about who the Messiah is.
avoid-legalism-caricature.claim: The caricature — Judaism as joyless rule-keeping to earn salvation, set against Christian grace — is false on the sources, and it destroys your credibility. Rabbinic Judaism is soaked in grace. Election comes before obligation: 'All Israel has a share in the world to come' (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1). The High Holy Day liturgy pleads Avinu Malkeinu — 'be gracious to us and answer us, for we have no deeds.' The Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34:6-7 anchor those days. And chesed, covenant love, is arguably the central divine attribute in the whole Hebrew Bible. E. P. Sanders demolished the caricature academically in 1977, coining the phrase 'covenantal nomism': Jews keep Torah as a response to a gracious God, not as wages earned. The real disagreement is narrower and worth stating precisely. It is not grace versus works. It is the ground of atonement — whether repentance is enough, or whether God has provided a sacrifice.

avoid-gematria-bible-codes.response: Defenders — Witztum's replies, and the Meru Foundation — argue that Brendan McKay's counter-experiments used looser rules than the original study, and that some equidistant-letter phenomena survive scrutiny. But the methodological point is conceded even by sympathetic statisticians. The results are extremely sensitive to the choices the researcher makes, they cannot be falsified in practice, and the same effects reproduce in ordinary secular books. No rabbinic authority rests doctrine on codes. Classical gematria, as in the Baal HaTurim, is homiletic ornament and never proof — a distinction the tradition itself is careful about.
avoid-gematria-bible-codes.rationale: Do not use it. Codes and gematria invert this section's entire method. The Messiah case rests on the plain sense of public texts — the same verses the Targums and the Talmud discuss — read the way Jesus himself argued on the Emmaus road, 'from Moses and all the prophets' in Luke 24:27. A hidden-message argument concedes that the plain text is not enough. It also cannot be checked, which is the one thing every argument on this site is supposed to be.
avoid-gematria-bible-codes.claim: Arguments from letter-skipping codes, gematria sums and Torah-code 'discoveries' should be banned from this case entirely. The flagship academic claim was published by Witztum, Rips and Rosenberg in Statistical Science in 1994. It was formally answered in the same journal in 1999 by McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel and Kalai, who showed the result was 'fatally defective' — an artifact of flexible data selection. Answering a challenge from the journalist Michael Drosnin, McKay then 'found' the Rabin assassination and other encoded prophecies in Moby-Dick. The method proves anything, and therefore nothing. Given enough freedom in spelling, skip distance and name choice, any long text yields any message. Christian use of codes borrows the least defensible fringe of Jewish mysticism to prop up a case that — as the rest of this section shows — stands perfectly well on the plain text, the Targums and the Talmud read in context.
